question:
Select the appropriate synonym for the underlined word.

Don't sound so excited
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. eager.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Excited" means very enthusiastic, thrilled and eagerly looking forward to something. (उत्साहित / रोमांचित)

◦ Its closest synonym among the given options is "eager", which means keenly interested and impatient to do something.

◦ Correct: Don't sound so excited (eager).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "casual" means relaxed, informal or unconcerned — the very opposite of being excited.

• Option 2 "composed" means calm, self-controlled and unruffled — an antonym of excited.

• Option 4 "tired" means weary or exhausted, which has no connection with excitement.

NOTE

• Synonyms of excited: eager, thrilled, enthusiastic, animated, agitated, exhilarated.

• Antonyms of excited: calm, composed, indifferent, apathetic, unmoved.

• SSC frequently tests such adjective pairs — remember eager (उत्सुक) vs weary (थका हुआ).

question: Four sentences are given, out of which three have spelling errors. Choose the sentence with all correctly spelt words.
option_1: What was the begining of the dispute?
option_2: There is no comparision between the two books.
option_4: I got selected in D category.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. I got selected in D category.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Only Option 4 contains no spelling error — every word ("got", "selected", "category") is correctly spelt.

• The other three sentences each carry a misspelt word:

◦ Option 1: "begining" is wrong; the correct spelling is "beginning" (BE + GIN + NING — the final "n" of "begin" is doubled before "-ing").

◦ Option 2: "comparision" is wrong; the correct spelling is "comparison" (COM + PAR + I + SON — no "i" after "ris").

◦ Option 3: "handlled" and "cooly" are both wrong; the correct forms are "handled" (single "l") and "coolly" (cool + ly, with a double "l").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Doubling rule: in a word ending with a single vowel + single consonant with the stress on the last syllable, the consonant is doubled before "-ing/-ed" — begin → beginning, refer → referring.

• Adverb rule: when an adjective already ends in "-l", adding "-ly" gives a double l — cool → coolly, real → really, full → fully (exception: full → fully drops one l).

NOTE

• Commonly misspelt SSC words: beginning, occurrence, committee, accommodation, embarrass, maintenance, privilege, questionnaire, comparison.

question:
Select the appropriate synonym for the underlined word.

You look around and you see green, happy plants.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. blissful.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Happy" means feeling or showing pleasure, joy and contentment. (प्रसन्न / खुश)

◦ The closest synonym here is "blissful", which means full of joy and perfect happiness.

◦ Correct: You look around and you see green, happy (blissful) plants — i.e., plants that look thriving and joyful.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "mourning" means grieving over a death or loss — an antonym of happy.

• Option 2 "nascent" means just coming into existence or beginning to develop; it describes a stage, not a mood.

• Option 4 "gloomy" means dark, dismal and depressed — again the opposite of happy.

NOTE

• Synonyms of happy: blissful, cheerful, delighted, elated, jubilant, content, joyful.

• Antonyms of happy: sad, gloomy, mournful, dejected, miserable, sorrowful.

• "Bliss" (noun) = perfect happiness; "blissful" (adjective) = extremely happy.

question:
Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.

Fred and George had / bewitched there trunks to fly downstairs to / save the bother of carrying them.
option_1: bewitched there trunks to fly downstairs to
option_2: save the bother of carrying them.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. bewitched there trunks to fly downstairs to.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error is the wrong homophone "there". The sentence needs the possessive adjective "their" (belonging to them), not the adverb of place "there".

◦ Correct segment: bewitched their trunks to fly downstairs to.

◦ Full correct sentence: Fred and George had bewitched their trunks to fly downstairs to save the bother of carrying them.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "save the bother of carrying them." is correct — "save the bother of + V-ing" means to avoid the trouble of doing something.

• Option 3 "Fred and George had" is correct — a plural subject with the past perfect auxiliary "had".

• Option 4 "No error" is wrong because a clear homophone error exists.

NOTE

• Homophone trio: their (possessive — their books), there (place — sit there), they're (they are).

• Other SSC homophone pairs: your/you're, its/it's, whose/who's, principal/principle, stationary/stationery.

question:
Select the most appropriate word for the given group of words.

Information, especially of a biased or misleading nature, used to promote a political cause or point of view
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Propaganda.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Propaganda" is exactly information, especially of a biased or misleading nature, used to promote a political cause or point of view. (दुष्प्रचार / प्रचार)

◦ Example: The regime used radio broadcasts as propaganda to influence public opinion.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Welter" means a large, confused and disordered mass or jumble of things.

• Option 3 "Potable" is an adjective meaning fit to drink (potable water = पीने योग्य जल).

• Option 4 "Orchard" is a piece of land planted with fruit trees.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutes: propagandist (one who spreads propaganda), demagogue (a leader who appeals to popular prejudice), rhetoric (persuasive but often insincere speech), canard (a false rumour).

question:
Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.

Although people had been on watch and / the watchkeepers were very, very tired, / everyone were up and buzzing.
option_3: Although people had been on watch and
option_4: the watchkeepers were very, very tired,
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. everyone were up and buzzing.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Everyone" is an indefinite pronoun that is always singular, so it must take the singular verb "was", not the plural "were".

◦ Correct segment: everyone was up and buzzing.

◦ Full correct sentence: Although people had been on watch and the watchkeepers were very, very tired, everyone was up and buzzing.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 3 "Although people had been on watch and" is correct — plural subject "people" with "had been".

• Option 4 "the watchkeepers were very, very tired," is correct — plural subject with the plural verb "were".

• Option 2 "No Error" is wrong because the subject–verb agreement error is clear.

NOTE

• Always singular: everyone, everybody, everything, someone, somebody, anyone, anybody, no one, nobody, each, either, neither.

◦ Everyone is invited. / Each of the boys has a bag. / Neither of them was present.

question:
Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'

Your body will respond by/ getting more muscular and/ strong before you know it.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. strong before you know it.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence uses two adjectives joined by "and" after the verb "getting", so both must be in the same (comparative) degree — the principle of parallelism.

◦ Since the first is "more muscular" (comparative), the second must also be comparative: "stronger", not the positive "strong".

◦ Correct segment: stronger before you know it.

◦ Full correct sentence: Your body will respond by getting more muscular and stronger before you know it.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 3 "Your body will respond by" is correct — "respond by + V-ing".

• Option 4 "getting more muscular and" is correct — "more muscular" is the proper comparative of the long adjective "muscular".

• Option 2 "No error" is wrong because the degrees are not parallel.

NOTE

• Degree rules: one-syllable adjectives add -er/-est (strong – stronger – strongest); adjectives of three or more syllables take more/most (muscular – more muscular – most muscular). Never mix a positive with a comparative in a parallel structure.

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

Crude
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Ripe.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Crude" means raw, unrefined, unprocessed or immature (as in crude oil, a crude remark, a crude sketch). (कच्चा / अपरिष्कृत)

◦ Its antonym among the options is "ripe", which means fully developed, mature and ready — the opposite of raw/unripe.

◦ Example: Crude oil must be refined; a ripe mango is ready to eat.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Beastly" means brutal, savage or very unpleasant — closer in flavour to crude, not opposite to it.

• Option 3 "Stubble" is a noun meaning the short stalks of grain left in a field after harvesting, or short bristly facial hair.

• Option 4 "Intense" means extreme in strength or degree, which is unrelated to refinement.

NOTE

• Synonyms of crude: raw, unrefined, rough, coarse, vulgar, rudimentary.

• Antonyms of crude: refined, polished, ripe, mature, sophisticated, cultured.

question:
Fill in the blank with the most appropriate option.

'Well, that was ______ good,' said Harper.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. pretty.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank comes before the adjective "good", so it needs an intensifying adverb (a degree word), not another adjective.

• "Pretty" is commonly used informally as an adverb of degree meaning "fairly / quite / rather".

◦ Correct: 'Well, that was pretty good,' said Harper. (= that was quite good) (काफी अच्छा)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Options 1 "pleasing", 2 "gorgeous" and 3 "beautiful" are all adjectives; placing an adjective directly before another adjective ("pleasing good", "beautiful good") is ungrammatical.

• Only "pretty" doubles as both an adjective (a pretty dress) and an adverb (pretty tired, pretty sure).

NOTE

• Other adverbs of degree used before adjectives: quite, rather, fairly, really, very, extremely, somewhat, awfully.

◦ "It's pretty cold today." / "She was rather upset.".

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

She has a large, ________ sympathy and absolute fairness of temper.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. generous.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank sits beside the positive adjective "large" and the phrase "absolute fairness of temper", so the missing word must also be positive and large-hearted.

• "Generous" means kind, liberal, big-hearted and willing to give. It pairs naturally with "large sympathy". (उदार / दयालु)

◦ Correct: She has a large, generous sympathy and absolute fairness of temper.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "mean" means unkind, petty or miserly — the direct opposite of the required sense.

• Option 2 "sparing" means using or giving very little; "sparing sympathy" contradicts "large".

• Option 4 "thrifty" means careful with money — a virtue about spending, not about sympathy.

NOTE

• Synonyms of generous: liberal, magnanimous, benevolent, charitable, bountiful, open-handed.

• Antonyms of generous: mean, stingy, miserly, niggardly, parsimonious.

question:
Select the word segment that substitutes (replaces) the bracketed word segment correctly and completes the sentence meaningfully. Select the option 'no correction required' if the sentence is correct as given.

He lost his temper (by a driver) flashed her headlights as he overtook.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. after a driver.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence needs a subordinating conjunction of time to link the two clauses "He lost his temper" and "a driver flashed her headlights as he overtook".

• "After" correctly shows that the driver's action came first and the loss of temper followed.

◦ Correct: He lost his temper after a driver flashed her headlights as he overtook.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "No correction required" is wrong: "by a driver" makes the sentence meaningless — "lost his temper by a driver" is not English.

• Option 1 "afterwards a driver" is wrong — "afterwards" is an adverb, not a conjunction, so it cannot join two clauses.

• Option 3 "considering a driver" is wrong — "considering" introduces a reason/allowance ("considering his age"), which does not fit here.

NOTE

• Subordinating conjunctions of time: after, before, when, while, since, until, as soon as, once.

◦ "After" (conjunction) joins clauses; "afterwards" (adverb) stands alone: "He apologised afterwards.".

question:
Fill in the blank with the most appropriate option.

Sulochana, whose ______ I had so admired during the festival, seemed a different person.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. grace.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb "admired" demands a positive, admirable quality in the blank, and the contrast with "seemed a different person" shows the earlier impression was pleasing.

• "Grace" means elegance of movement, charm and refined courtesy — exactly the kind of quality one admires at a festival. (शालीनता / लावण्य)

◦ Correct: Sulochana, whose grace I had so admired during the festival, seemed a different person.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "polish" (refinement of manner) is positive but is normally admired in behaviour/finish, and is far weaker than "grace" in this context of a festival appearance.

• Option 2 "crudeness" means coarseness or lack of refinement — nobody "admires" crudeness.

• Option 4 "shadow" is a physical dark shape and cannot logically be admired here.

NOTE

• Words for elegance: grace, poise, elegance, charm, finesse, refinement.

• Note the relative pronoun "whose" is correctly used for possession with a person: "Sulochana, whose grace ..."..

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.

Fairly and squarely
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Honestly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "fairly and squarely" (also "fair and square") means honestly, justly and in a straightforward manner, without any cheating. (ईमानदारी से / निष्पक्ष रूप से)

◦ Example: He won the election fairly and squarely, with no manipulation of votes.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Suddenly" refers to speed/abruptness, not honesty.

• Option 2 "Rigorously" means strictly or thoroughly.

• Option 3 "Wholly" means entirely or completely — a possible secondary shade ("hit him fair and square"), but the primary sense tested here is honesty/fairness.

NOTE

• Related idioms: "above board" (open and honest), "on the level" (genuine), "play by the rules", "by fair means or foul" (by any method, honest or not).

question:
A sentence has been given with a blank to be filled with an appropriate option. Choose the correct alternative.

Your presence ______ both my brother and sister.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. affects.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank is the main verb of the sentence and the subject "Your presence" is singular, so a singular present-tense verb is required.

• "Affect" (verb) means to influence or have an impact on; with a singular subject it becomes "affects". (प्रभावित करना)

◦ Correct: Your presence affects both my brother and sister.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "affecting" is a participle and cannot stand alone as the finite verb (it would need "is affecting").

• Options 2 "effect" and 3 "effects" are normally nouns meaning "result/consequence", so they cannot serve as the verb here.

NOTE

• Golden rule: Affect = verb (to influence); Effect = noun (the result).

◦ Smoking affects health. / Smoking has a bad effect on health.

◦ Rare use: "effect" as a verb means "to bring about" — to effect a change.

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.

A container for housing honeybees
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Hive.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "hive" is a container or structure in which honeybees live and store honey (also called a beehive). (मधुमक्खी का छत्ता)

◦ Example: The beekeeper carefully opened the hive to collect the honeycomb.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Colonies" refers to the group of bees living together, not the container that houses them.

• Option 3 "Pack" is a collective noun for wolves/hounds/cards.

• Option 4 "Shoal" is a collective noun for fish.

NOTE

• Useful collective nouns: a swarm of bees, a flock of sheep/birds, a herd of cattle, a pride of lions, a shoal/school of fish, a pack of wolves, a litter of puppies.

• Animal homes: bees – hive, birds – nest, horses – stable, pigs – sty, rabbits – burrow, lions – den.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'no substitution required'.

(There's many a good tunes) played on an old violin.
option_2: There are many a good tunes
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. There are many good tunes.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• With the plural noun "tunes", the sentence needs the plural verb "are" and the plural quantifier "many".

◦ Correct: There are many good tunes played on an old violin.

• The original "There's many a good tunes" mixes two structures wrongly: "there's" (singular) with "tunes" (plural), and "many a" (which takes a singular noun) with the plural "tunes".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "No substitution required" is wrong because of the double error explained above.

• Option 2 "There are many a good tunes" still keeps the faulty "many a + plural noun".

• Option 3 "There's many good tune" wrongly uses "many" with a singular noun.

NOTE

• "Many a + singular noun + singular verb": Many a boy was absent.

• "Many + plural noun + plural verb": Many boys were absent.

• In "there is/there are" sentences, the verb agrees with the noun that follows it.

question: Choose the incorrectly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Staringg.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Staringg" is misspelt. The correct spelling is "staring" — the present participle of the verb "stare" (to look fixedly). (घूरना)

◦ Rule: a verb ending in a silent "e" drops the "e" before "-ing" and does not double the final consonant — stare → staring (not "staringg" or "starring" in this sense).

◦ Correct: He kept staring at the painting.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• "Grave" (serious; a burial place), "Leaf" (the flat green part of a plant) and "Blame" (to hold responsible) are all spelt correctly.

• Note the different word "starring" (with double r) which comes from "star" (to feature as the main actor) — a common confusion.

NOTE

• Spelling rules for "-ing": drop silent e (make → making, write → writing); double the consonant after a short stressed vowel (run → running, begin → beginning); no letter is ever doubled at the end of an "-ing" form.

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose 'No improvement' as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.

Even in time of natural disasters, the farmers had to pay their share of taxes.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. times of natural.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The plural noun "disasters" requires the plural expression "times", giving the standard idiom "in times of" (= during periods of).

◦ Correct: Even in times of natural disasters, the farmers had to pay their share of taxes.

• "In times of war / in times of crisis / in times of need" is the fixed usage; the singular "in time of" is archaic and does not agree with the plural "disasters".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "timer of natural" is meaningless — a "timer" is a device that measures time.

• Option 3 "times of naturally" is wrong: the adverb "naturally" cannot modify the noun "disasters"; an adjective ("natural") is needed.

• Option 4 "No improvement" is wrong because the number agreement must be corrected.

NOTE

• Fixed phrases: in times of trouble, at times, from time to time, in no time, in the nick of time.

• Adjective vs adverb: an adjective qualifies a noun (natural disaster), an adverb qualifies a verb/adjective/adverb (behaves naturally).

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym to substitute the bracketed word in the given sentence.

Similarly Sirius, the most (luminous) star in all the heavens, actually has a faint companion.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. gloomy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Luminous" means giving off light; bright, shining and radiant. (चमकीला / प्रकाशमान)

◦ Its antonym among the options is "gloomy", which means dark, dim and lacking light.

◦ Substituted: Similarly Sirius, the most gloomy star in all the heavens ... (the required opposite of luminous).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "excited" (thrilled) and Option 2 "miserable" (very unhappy) describe emotional states, not brightness.

• Option 3 "serious" (solemn, grave) is also unrelated to light.

• The sentence's own clue is "a faint companion" — "faint/dim/gloomy" all sit on the opposite side of "luminous".

NOTE

• Synonyms of luminous: bright, radiant, shining, glowing, brilliant, resplendent.

• Antonyms of luminous: dark, dim, gloomy, dull, murky, opaque.

• Static fact: Sirius (the Dog Star) is the brightest star in the night sky and is actually a binary system with a faint white-dwarf companion, Sirius B.

question:
The statement below has been given with bracketed text. Select the option with correct Idiom for the bracketed text.

He (made an irreversible change, that will greatly impact his life) when he got that huge tattoo on his back!
option_4: put a rose on his nose
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. crossed the Rubicon.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to cross the Rubicon" means to take an irrevocable step / to pass a point of no return that commits one to a course of action. (ऐसा कदम उठाना जिसे वापस न लिया जा सके)

◦ Correct: He crossed the Rubicon when he got that huge tattoo on his back!

• Origin: in 49 BC, Julius Caesar crossed the river Rubicon with his army against the Roman Senate's orders, making civil war inevitable — hence the sense of an irreversible decision.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "beat a dead horse" means to waste effort on a matter that is already settled or hopeless.

• Option 2 "play/become the devil's advocate" means to argue the opposite side merely for the sake of debate.

• Option 4 "put a rose on his nose" is not an English idiom at all.

NOTE

• Similar idioms of irreversibility: "burn one's boats/bridges", "the die is cast", "point of no return".

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

He (1) ______ his eyes. Moonlight was shining (2) ______ the bars on the window. And (3) ______ was goggling through the (4) ______ at him: a freckle-faced, red-haired, long-nosed someone. Ron Weasley was outside Harry's (5) ______.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No. 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. opened.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage is a past-tense narrative ("was shining", "was goggling"), so the blank needs the past form of the verb.

• The natural collocation with "eyes" is "opened his eyes" — the past tense of "open".

◦ Correct: He opened his eyes.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "open" is the base/present form and does not match the past-tense narration.

• Option 3 "close" gives the opposite sense and is also in the wrong tense (and one does not "close" one's eyes on waking to see moonlight).

• Option 1 "expanded" is used for size/volume (the balloon expanded), not for eyes being opened.

NOTE

• Collocations with "eyes": open/close/shut/rub/blink/roll one's eyes, keep an eye on, catch someone's eye.

• In cloze tests, first fix the tense from the surrounding verbs, then choose the word that collocates naturally.

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

He (1) ______ his eyes. Moonlight was shining (2) ______ the bars on the window. And (3) ______ was goggling through the (4) ______ at him: a freckle-faced, red-haired, long-nosed someone. Ron Weasley was outside Harry's (5) ______.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No. 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. through.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank needs a preposition of movement across/among an opening. Moonlight passes through the gaps of the bars into the room.

◦ Correct: Moonlight was shining through the bars on the window.

• "Shine through" is the standard collocation for light passing across a barrier or opening.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "though" is a conjunction meaning "although" — a classic spelling trap: though ≠ through.

• Option 4 "in" would need "in through" or a different structure; "shining in the bars" is not idiomatic.

• Option 1 "complete" is an adjective/verb and cannot function as a preposition here.

NOTE

• Distinguish: though (although), through (from one side to the other), thorough (complete/detailed), thought (past of think), trough (a long container).

• Prepositions with light: shine through a window, shine on a surface, shine into a room.

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

He (1) ______ his eyes. Moonlight was shining (2) ______ the bars on the window. And (3) ______ was goggling through the (4) ______ at him: a freckle-faced, red-haired, long-nosed someone. Ron Weasley was outside Harry's (5) ______.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No. 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. someone.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank is the subject of the verb "was goggling", so it must be a pronoun referring to a person.

• The passage itself confirms it: "a freckle-faced, red-haired, long-nosed someone" — the word is repeated later in the sentence.

◦ Correct: And someone was goggling through the bars at him.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "sometimes" is an adverb of frequency (occasionally) and cannot be a subject.

• Option 2 "somewhere" is an adverb of place.

• Option 4 "somewhat" is an adverb of degree (to some extent).

NOTE

• The "some-" family: someone/somebody (person), something (thing), somewhere (place), sometimes (frequency), somewhat (degree), someday (future time).

• "Goggle" means to stare with wide open eyes — hence "goggles" for protective eyewear.

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

He (1) ______ his eyes. Moonlight was shining (2) ______ the bars on the window. And (3) ______ was goggling through the (4) ______ at him: a freckle-faced, red-haired, long-nosed someone. Ron Weasley was outside Harry's (5) ______.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No. 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. bars.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word must refer back to something already mentioned in the passage. The previous sentence says the moonlight was shining through "the bars on the window", so the person is goggling through the same bars.

◦ Correct: And someone was goggling through the bars at him.

• Cohesion (referring back to a noun already introduced with "the") is the key to this blank.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Options 2 "verticals" and 4 "horizontals" are technical/geometrical terms and are not used for window bars.

• Option 3 "grills" (a grating) is loosely possible in Indian English, but it has not been mentioned earlier, so it breaks the cohesive link with "the bars".

NOTE

• In cloze passages, always scan the neighbouring sentences for a repeated or referred-to noun; the definite article "the" before a blank almost always points to something previously named.

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

He (1) ______ his eyes. Moonlight was shining (2) ______ the bars on the window. And (3) ______ was goggling through the (4) ______ at him: a freckle-faced, red-haired, long-nosed someone. Ron Weasley was outside Harry's (5) ______.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No. 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. window.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage has already established the setting: the moonlight shone through "the bars on the window", and someone was looking in through those bars. Therefore the person must be outside Harry's window.

◦ Correct: Ron Weasley was outside Harry's window.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "suitcase", Option 2 "toilet" and Option 4 "cupboard" cannot logically have barred openings through which moonlight enters a room and a face peers in.

• The logic chain is: bars → on the window → someone goggling through them → so the person is outside the window.

NOTE

• Closing blanks in a cloze are usually resolved by contextual consistency — pick the option that keeps the scene coherent with every earlier detail.
